areas_of_highest_concern:
Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to persist across the Dry Corridor, Alta Verapaz, and the Altiplano in September, driven by previous years' poor harvests among smallholder farmers, unfavorable
weather forecasts for the upcoming primera season, and prolonged market dependence amid an extended lean season. Although primera harvests will begin to flow into the markets in September, localized
delays in planting and below-average yields for smallholder farmers are unlikely to substantially reduce reliance on coping strategies.

Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes are expected to persist in areas of Port-au-Prince and among IDPs through September. The continued expansion of gang violence and resulting displacement will continue
to disrupt livelihoods and reduce household food access. Food prices will likely remain well above average, but the spring harvest is anticipated to improve food access and availability. Widespread Crisis (IPC
Phase 3) outcomes are most likely to persist across most of the country as livelihood opportunities remain constrained by insecurity.

In pastoral areas, Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected through September, driven by declines in livestock body conditions and productivity due to atypically dry conditions, resulting in below-average
incomes and food access. Marginal agricultural areas, specifically Kitui, Makueni, and Lamu counties, are expected to improve to Stressed (IPC Phase 2 outcomes) from June to September, as favorable early
2026 rainfall is expected to support an average harvest in marginal agricultural areas starting in June, ahead of the dry harvest in July. Refugee populations are also of concern.

areas_of_highest_concern:
By September, the green harvest in southern Mali is expected to improve food security locally. However, conflict across northern and central regions will continue to significantly restrict household access to
food and income. Emergency (IPC Phase 4) is expected in Ménaka, where insecurity severely disrupts markets and livelihoods. Crisis (IPC Phase 3) will persist in conflict-affected northern and central regions,
particularly Mopti, Tombouctou, Gao, and Kidal. Needs will likely remain higher than last year due to an early lean season, disrupted harvests, and displacement linked to escalating insecurity and the fuel crisis.

areas_of_highest_concern:
Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected in central and southern areas in September, supported by own-produced food stocks from the anticipated average 2026 harvest. Seasonal declines in food
prices, coupled with increased income-earning opportunities, are likely to improve food access for poor households; however, many poor households will not be able to meet their non-food needs.

In September, Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected in areas where the 2025/26 agricultural season was disrupted due to weather and conflict shocks. In the north, conflict and displacement disrupted
households' ability to engage in the agricultural season, which is expected to drive low production and continued reliance on markets in affected areas. Meanwhile, in southern and central Mozambique, areas
worst-affected by flooding and localized dry spells during the growing period are likely to face difficulty accessing own-produced food due to harvest losses.

areas_of_highest_concern:
Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected in Tillabéry, Diffa, and Tahoua due to conflict, which is also expanding to Dosso, causing population displacement, disrupting market functionality and supply, and
affecting livelihoods. In September, the lean season’s peak, poor households are likely to face high food prices and depleted food stocks, increasing market dependence.

Across northern Nigeria, escalating conflict, displacement, and constrained market access will sustain high food assistance needs through August. Needs are expected to decline slightly in September as the
harvest becomes available and market functioning improves seasonally. Despite this temporary improvement, ongoing insecurity, localized flooding, and persistently high food prices will continue to drive
food consumption deficits. Emergency (IPC Phase 4) is likely to persist in the worst-affected inaccessible areas of the North East. Widespread Crisis (IPC Phase 3) is expected across the rest of the north.

areas_of_highest_concern:
Following key shifts in conflict dynamics and population movement in early 2026, the thresholds for Famine (IPC Phase 5) are no longer met or expected to be met; however, widespread Emergency (IPC Phase
4) with populations in Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) are expected to persist, with a credible risk of renewed Famine (IPC Phase 5) if conflict and/or levels of besiegement increase beyond what is expected and
isolate households from food, including humanitarian assistance. The change from Famine (IPC Phase 5) to a credible risk of Famine (IPC Phase 5) does not reflect substantial improvement, but is driven by
several factors: the scale of deaths that likely occurred under the extreme siege conditions between mid-2025 and January 2026; large-scale displacement out of the towns; the breaking of the sieges in late
January and early February that facilitated the arrival of market and humanitarian supplies; and the expectation that the reestablishment of siege conditions will not escalate to the same intensity as in 2025.

Near-average gu rains and harvests are expected to relatively improve food access in agropastoral areas, but debt repayments will burden poor households and sustain high food assistance needs. In pastoral
areas, successive below-average rainfall seasons, characterized by high livestock losses, weak herd reproduction, and low milk availability, are expected to limit recovery. Emergency (IPC Phase 4) is likely to
continue in central and northern pastoral areas and across several IDP settlements. If April-June gu rainfall is unfavorable, however, both the scale and severity of food insecurity would likely increase.

Needs are expected to remain at their peak in September despite the start of the harvest, driven by anticipated severe conflict- and flood-related disruptions to trade flows and livelihood activities, including
agricultural production. North-central Jonglei and southern Upper Nile remain the areas of highest concern, particularly among the displaced populations. Escalating conflict, displacement, and severe
humanitarian access constraints are driving a credible risk of Famine (IPC Phase 5) in six counties. These areas are already experiencing high levels of hunger, acute malnutrition, and cholera. If conflict
escalates and isolates populations, preventing access to local food sources and humanitarian assistance for a prolonged period of time, then Famine (IPC Phase 5) would likely occur.

Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected in September as the primera harvest becomes more available, despite localized delays in planting. Seasonal improvements for smallholder farmers, especially in
the Eastern Dry Corridor, will likely be limited; however, most households are likely to be able to meet their minimal food needs through sustainable coping strategies.

areas_of_highest_concern:
During the ongoing January to April lean season, drought-like conditions, persistent insecurity, and a weakening economy will continue to restrict households' access to food across Syria. While the harvest will

improvements will likely be concentrated in the coastal governorates, where seasonal income-generating opportunities and localized harvests support Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes.
